faqs.answer: The milk. A latte is 1:5 espresso to milk with thin foam, in an 8 to 12 oz cup. A cappuccino is equal thirds of espresso, steamed milk, and thick foam, in a 5 to 6 oz cup.
faqs.question: What is the difference between a latte and a cappuccino?

faqs.answer: 60 to 65 C, or 140 to 150 F. Hotter than that and the milk scalds and tastes flat. A thermometer takes the guesswork out.

howToSteps.name: Pull a double shot
howToSteps.text: Dose 18 g of fine coffee and pull 36 g of espresso in 25 to 30 seconds, straight into the cup.

howToSteps.name: Steam the milk
howToSteps.text: Steam 180 g of cold whole milk to 60 to 65 C, with just a thin layer of foam, about a centimetre. Wipe the steam wand clean.

howToSteps.name: Pour slowly
howToSteps.text: Pour the milk into the espresso in a slow, steady stream, holding the jug close to the cup. Finish with the thin foam on top.

howToSteps.name: Serve straight away
howToSteps.text: A latte goes cold fast and the foam breaks down. Serve it as soon as it is poured.

title: Espresso to Milk Ratio for a Latte
tutorial: A latte is the milkiest drink on the espresso menu: one part espresso to five parts steamed milk, with just a thin layer of foam on top. A double shot of 36 g takes 180 g of milk, which fills a 10 oz cup.

The ratio moves with the cup. An 8 oz latte with a double shot works out to about 1:3, and a 12 oz latte to 1:5, because the shot stays the same while the milk grows. The 1:5 figure is the standard for a regular 10 to 12 oz latte, and it is the one most guides cite.

Start with the espresso. A double shot is 18 g of finely ground coffee pulled to 36 g of liquid espresso in 25 to 30 seconds. Weigh the shot if you can: a shot that runs long tastes thin, and a shot that runs short tastes sour, and neither makes a good latte however much milk you add.

Steam the milk to 60 to 65 C, which is 140 to 150 F. That is hot enough to taste sweet and silky, and cool enough not to scald. Whole milk steams best because the fat carries the texture. The foam on a latte should be thin, about a centimetre, not the thick cap of a cappuccino.

Pour the milk slowly into the espresso, holding the jug close to the cup so the milk slides under the crema instead of sitting on top. A latte is a milk drink with coffee in it, not the other way round, so if the cup tastes too strong, add milk before you blame the beans.
